claim: Selective packaging of HIV-1 genomic RNA (gRNA) requires the presence of a cis-acting RNA element called the 'packaging signal' (Ψ).
source: Selective packaging of HIV-1 genomic RNA (gRNA) requires the presence of a cis-acting RNA element called the 'packaging signal' (Ψ).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: At physiological ionic strength, Gag binds with very similar, nanomolar affinities to both Ψ-containing and control RNAs.
source: At physiological ionic strength, Gag binds with very similar, nanomolar affinities to both Ψ-containing and control RNAs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: Addition of excess competing tRNA, introducing mutations in Gag, or raising the ionic strength reveals high specificity for Ψ.
source: We challenged these interactions by adding excess competing tRNA; introducing mutations in Gag; or raising the ionic strength. These modifications all revealed high specificity for Ψ.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 3, 5, 6, and 7-9.

claim: The specificity of Gag for Ψ is obscured in physiological salt by non-specific, predominantly electrostatic interactions.
source: This specificity is evidently obscured in physiological salt by non-specific, predominantly electrostatic interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that specificity is revealed when electrostatic interactions are reduced.

claim: Nonspecific binding activity was attenuated by mutations in the MA, CA, and NC domains, including CA mutations disrupting Gag-Gag interaction.
source: This nonspecific activity was attenuated by mutations in the MA, CA, and NC domains, including CA mutations disrupting Gag-Gag interaction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with mutant Gag proteins shown in Figures 5, 6, and 9.

claim: gRNA is selectively packaged because binding to Ψ nucleates virion assembly with particular efficiency.
source: We propose that gRNA is selectively packaged because binding to Ψ nucleates virion assembly with particular efficiency.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings and represents speculation about the biological significance.

claim: Immature virions of HIV-1 and other retroviruses are assembled from the viral Gag polyprotein.
source: Immature virions of HIV-1 and other retroviruses are assembled from the viral Gag polyprotein.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of retrovirology.

claim: The Gag precursor protein consists of matrix (MA), capsid (CA), nucleocapsid (NC) and p6 domains, as well as two spacer peptides (SP1 and SP2) flanking the NC domain.
source: This precursor protein consists of matrix (MA), capsid (CA), nucleocapsid (NC) and p6 domains, as well as two spacer peptides (SP1 and SP2) flanking the NC domain.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about HIV-1 Gag.

claim: The MA domain binds Gag to the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: The MA domain binds Gag to the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (Zhou et al., 1994; Chukkapalli et al., 2010; Barros et al., 2016), although in the cytoplasm it is bound to RNA (Kutluay et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the cytoplasm, the MA domain is bound to RNA.
source: The MA domain binds Gag to the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (Zhou et al., 1994; Chukkapalli et al., 2010; Barros et al., 2016), although in the cytoplasm it is bound to RNA (Kutluay et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kutluay et al., 2014.

claim: The CA domain (together with SP1) drives virion assembly.
source: the CA domain (together with SP1) drives virion assembly (Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2007; Worthylake et al., 1999; Datta et al., 2011a; Datta et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The NC domain is required for incorporation of nucleic acids.
source: the NC domain is required for incorporation of nucleic acids (the two zinc fingers in this domain are necessary for selective RNA packaging) (Aldovini and Young, 1990; Gorelick et al., 1990; Cimarelli et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The two zinc fingers in the NC domain are necessary for selective RNA packaging.
source: the NC domain is required for incorporation of nucleic acids (the two zinc fingers in this domain are necessary for selective RNA packaging) (Aldovini and Young, 1990; Gorelick et al., 1990; Cimarelli et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The p6 domain interacts with the host-cell machinery to release virions from the cell.
source: and the p6 domain interacts with the host-cell machinery to release virions from the cell (Freed, 2002; Usami et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: All retrovirus particles contain RNA.
source: As far as is known, all retrovirus particles also contain RNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Addition of RNA to recombinant Gag protein in vitro leads to its assembly into virus-like particles (VLPs).
source: In fact, addition of RNA to recombinant Gag protein in vitro leads to its assembly into virus-like particles (VLPs) (Campbell and Rein, 1999; Campbell et al., 2001; Gross et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cooperative binding to nucleic acid brings Gag molecules into close proximity with each other, thereby nucleating virion assembly.
source: We have suggested that cooperative binding to nucleic acid brings Gag molecules into close proximity with each other, thereby nucleating virion assembly (Rein et al., 2011; Datta et al., 2011a; Datta et al., 2015; Comas-Garcia et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SP1 undergoes a conformational change when two or more copies are closely juxtaposed.
source: In particular, we have found that SP1 undergoes a conformational change when two or more copies are closely juxtaposed (Datta et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The conformational change in SP1 plausibly causes the exposure of interfaces in Gag required for particle assembly.
source: It is plausible that this change causes the exposure of interfaces in Gag required for particle assembly.
evidence: This is speculation based on previous findings.

claim: Almost any single-stranded nucleic acid can support virus-like particle (VLP) assembly in vitro.
source: Almost any single-stranded nucleic acid can support virus-like particle (VLP) assembly in vitro (Campbell and Rein, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: In infected cells, the full-length viral RNA (genomic RNA or gRNA) is encapsidated with very high selectivity.
source: Nonetheless in infected cells, the full-length viral RNA (genomic RNA or gRNA) is encapsidated with very high selectivity.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: When Gag is expressed in mammalian cells lacking gRNA, it assembles into VLPs containing a nearly random assortment of cellular mRNA molecules.
source: However, when Gag is expressed in mammalian cells lacking gRNA, it assembles into VLPs containing a nearly random assortment of cellular mRNA molecules (Rulli et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The 'structural' role of RNA in virion assembly can be provided by either gRNA or by cellular RNAs.
source: Thus, the 'structural' role of RNA in virion assembly can be provided by either gRNA or by cellular RNAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the previous statement about VLP assembly with cellular RNAs.

claim: In infected cells, the gRNA is competing with a large excess of cellular RNAs and spliced viral RNAs for encapsidation.
source: In infected cells, the gRNA is competing with a large excess of cellular RNAs and spliced viral RNAs for encapsidation, and evidently has a strong advantage in this competition.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The gRNA has a strong advantage in competition with cellular RNAs and spliced viral RNAs for encapsidation.
source: In infected cells, the gRNA is competing with a large excess of cellular RNAs and spliced viral RNAs for encapsidation, and evidently has a strong advantage in this competition.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective packaging of gRNA.

claim: The HIV-1 gRNA contains a cis-acting RNA element called the 'packaging signal' ('Ψ') that is required for its selective packaging during virion assembly.
source: As in all retroviruses, the HIV-1 gRNA contains a cis-acting RNA element called the 'packaging signal' ('Ψ') that is required for its selective packaging during virion assembly (Aldovini and Young, 1990; Lever et al., 1989; Clavel and Orenstein, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The packaging signal consists of several hundred nucleotides in the 5'-untranslated region (UTR) and part of the Gag open reading frame.
source: This signal consists of several hundred nucleotides in the 5'-untranslated region (UTR) and part of the Gag open reading frame.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of Ψ.

claim: Under physiologically relevant salt concentrations, Gag binds to Ψ and non-Ψ RNAs with very similar, nanomolar affinities.
source: However, we show here that under physiologically relevant salt concentrations, this protein binds to Ψ and non-Ψ RNAs with very similar, nanomolar affinities.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: A simple high-affinity scenario is unlikely to explain the packaging selectivity observed in vivo.
source: Thus, it seems unlikely that a simple high-affinity scenario could explain the packaging selectivity observed in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that affinities are similar for Ψ and non-Ψ RNAs.

claim: At near-physiological ionic strengths the affinities of Gag for different RNAs are virtually indistinguishable.
source: As noted above, we find that at near-physiological ionic strengths the affinities of Gag for these different RNAs are virtually indistinguishable.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: When the strength of Gag-Gag and/or Gag-RNA interactions is modulated, Gag binds with high specificity to a Ψ-containing RNA.
source: However, when the strength of Gag-Gag and/or Gag-RNA interactions is modulated, Gag binds with high specificity to a Ψ-containing RNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with mutant proteins and competition experiments.

claim: There is a much larger contribution of specific binding with Ψ compared to non-Ψ RNAs.
source: While there are both specific and non-specific components in binding to any RNA, there is a much larger contribution of specific binding with Ψ.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing differential effects of challenges on Ψ vs non-Ψ binding.

claim: Strong Gag-Gag interactions make a major contribution to the non-specific component of RNA binding.
source: Unexpectedly, strong Gag-Gag interactions make a major contribution to the non-specific component.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with WM mutant Gag shown in Figure 6.

claim: The type and strength of Gag-Gag and Gag-RNA interactions during binding might lead to preferential encapsidation of gRNA.
source: We suggest a novel general mechanism by which the type and strength of Gag-Gag and Gag-RNA interactions during binding might lead to preferential encapsidation of gRNA.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Addition of RNA to Gag can lead to assembly of VLPs, complicating the measurement of a dissociation constant (KD) for the binding.
source: As noted in the Introduction, addition of RNA to Gag can lead to assembly of VLPs, complicating the measurement of a dissociation constant (KD) for the binding.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration based on known behavior of Gag.

claim: Most biophysical techniques require high Gag concentrations (micromolar regime) at which Gag/RNA complexes will associate into virus-like-particles.
source: In fact, most biophysical techniques (e.g., sedimentation experiments or isothermal calorimetry) require high Gag concentrations (micromolar regime); at these concentrations Gag/RNA complexes will associate into virus-like-particles.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of biophysical techniques and Gag behavior.

claim: FCS was used at low RNA concentrations where association of Gag/RNA complexes into VLPs or other large structures is not thermodynamically favorable.
source: We have circumvented this problem by using FCS, in which the concentration of the fluorophore-tagged RNA is low enough that association of Gag/RNA complexes into VLPs or other large structures is not thermodynamically favorable.
evidence: This is a methodological approach described by the authors.

claim: The HIV-1 Ψ RNA was studied in both monomeric and dimeric forms.
source: As many lines of evidence indicate that only dimeric gRNA is selectively packaged (Moore et al., 2009), we studied the HIV-1 Ψ RNA in both monomeric and dimeric forms (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a methodological choice supported by citation.

claim: Only dimeric gRNA is selectively packaged.
source: As many lines of evidence indicate that only dimeric gRNA is selectively packaged (Moore et al., 2009), we studied the HIV-1 Ψ RNA in both monomeric and dimeric forms (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Binding of Gag to the tested RNAs resulted in an increase in the diffusion coefficient (D) of the RNAs.
source: Binding of Gag to the tested RNAs resulted in an increase in the D of the RNAs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The diffusion coefficient for each RNA increases as the concentration of Gag is increased, reaching a plateau at ≈ 50–100 nM Gag for HIV-1 Ψ (monomeric and dimeric) and ≈ 200–250 nM Gag with MoMLV Ψ and GRPE RNAs.
source: In Figure 1a it can be seen that the D for each RNA increases as the concentration of Gag is increased, reaching a plateau at ≈ 50–100 nM Gag in the case of HIV-1 Ψ (monomeric and dimeric) and ≈ 200–250 nM Gag with MoMLV Ψ and GRPE RNAs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The dimerization efficiency of HIV-1 Ψ RNA was ≈ 90%.
source: (Figure 1—figure supplement 4 shows that the diffusion coefficients (D) of the monomeric and dimeric HIV-1 Ψ RNAs were different enough to be resolved from each other by FCS and that the dimerization efficiency was ≈ 90%).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The binding of Gag results in a decrease in the hydrodynamic radius of the RNA.
source: Thus, the binding of Gag results in a decrease in the hydrodynamic radius of the RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the increase in diffusion coefficient.

claim: Binding of Gag to the RNA causes a collapse in the RNA.
source: This was somewhat unexpected, as the Gag/RNA complexes must have greater masses than the free RNAs, and implies that binding of Gag to the RNA causes a collapse in the RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the increase in diffusion coefficient despite increased mass.

claim: The increase in the diffusion coefficient is not due to RNA degradation.
source: The increase in the diffusion coefficient is not due to RNA degradation; upon digestion of the Gag/RNA complexes with Proteinase K, the D of the labeled RNA reverts to that of naked RNA (see Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Capsid proteins of other RNA viruses also cause RNA collapse.
source: Capsid proteins of other RNA viruses also cause RNA collapse (Borodavka et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gag-induced RNA collapse is a cooperative process.
source: Therefore, Gag-induced RNA collapse is evidently a cooperative process.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing Hill coefficients greater than 1 in Figure 1B.

claim: The exponent associated with the Gag concentration required for RNA collapse was greater than one for all RNAs (between 1.7 and 3.4).
source: the exponent associated with the Gag concentration required for RNA collapse (analogous to the Hill coefficient (nH) in the Hill Equation for cooperative binding) was greater than one for all RNAs (between 1.7 and 3.4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The fluorescence of the RNAs is reduced by addition of Gag.
source: As mentioned before, the fluorescence of the RNAs is reduced by addition of Gag (see Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At 0.2 M NaCl, the affinities of Gag for the different RNAs are all very similar to each other.
source: It is obvious that, at 0.2 M NaCl, the affinities of Gag for the different RNAs are all very similar to each other.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: The concentrations of Gag needed to bind half of the RNAs in solution for the different RNAs are all within a factor of two of each other.
source: That is, the concentrations of Gag needed to bind half of the RNAs in solution for the different RNAs are all within a factor of two of each other.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The data is best described when fitted with a simple cooperative model (Hill equation).
source: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 is a representative example that shows that the data is best described when fitted with a simple cooperative model (Hill equation).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The KDs obtained ranged from 21 nM for dimeric HIV-1 Ψ to 44 nM for GRPE.
source: Table 1 shows that the KDs obtained ranged from 21 nM for dimeric HIV-1 Ψ to 44 nM for GRPE.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The Hill coefficients (nH) derived from binding curves varied between 1.6 and 2.5.
source: Furthermore, the nHs derived from these curves varied between 1.6 and 2.5 (see Table 1), implying that cooperativity is not a specific property of the RNA but a general characteristic of Gag.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Cooperativity is not a specific property of the RNA but a general characteristic of Gag.
source: Furthermore, the nHs derived from these curves varied between 1.6 and 2.5 (see Table 1), implying that cooperativity is not a specific property of the RNA but a general characteristic of Gag.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar Hill coefficients for different RNAs.

claim: Under the experimental conditions, Gag binds to RNAs with high affinity but low specificity.
source: Finally, we see that under these experimental conditions Gag binds to RNAs with high affinity but low specificity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: The difference in the binding affinity between the dimeric HIV-1 Ψ and the control RNAs appears insufficient to explain selective RNA packaging in vivo.
source: The difference in the binding affinity between the dimeric HIV-1 Ψ and the control RNAs appears insufficient to explain selective RNA packaging in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the small differences in KD values.

claim: Addition of competitor RNAs causes only a modest reduction in the binding to the monomeric and dimeric HIV-1 Ψ RNAs.
source: As shown in Figure 3, the binding curves obtained in the presence of tRNAs showed that addition of these competitor RNAs causes only a modest reduction in the binding to the monomeric and dimeric HIV-1 Ψ RNAs
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Addition of competitor tRNAs causes a somewhat larger reduction in binding to MoMLV Ψ.
source: As shown in Figure 3, the binding curves obtained in the presence of tRNAs showed that addition of these competitor RNAs causes only a modest reduction in the binding to the monomeric and dimeric HIV-1 Ψ RNAs, a somewhat larger reduction in binding to MoMLV Ψ
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Addition of competitor tRNAs causes a drastic decrease in the binding to GRPE RNA.
source: As shown in Figure 3, the binding curves obtained in the presence of tRNAs showed that addition of these competitor RNAs causes only a modest reduction in the binding to the monomeric and dimeric HIV-1 Ψ RNAs, a somewhat larger reduction in binding to MoMLV Ψ, and a drastic decrease in the binding to GRPE RNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The apparent affinities of Gag for both forms of HIV-1 Ψ were reduced roughly ≈2-fold by the addition of the tRNAs.
source: The KDs derived from these curves (Table 1) show that the apparent affinities of Gag for both forms of HIV-1 Ψ were reduced roughly ≈2-fold by the addition of the tRNAs
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The apparent affinities of Gag for MoMLV Ψ and GRPE were reduced ≈4.5 and 7-fold, respectively, by addition of tRNAs.
source: The KDs derived from these curves (Table 1) show that the apparent affinities of Gag for both forms of HIV-1 Ψ were reduced roughly ≈2-fold by the addition of the tRNAs, while those for the MoMLV Ψ and GRPE were reduced ≈4.5 and 7-fold, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Gag has a higher binding specificity for the HIV-1 Ψ than for the control RNAs.
source: These data show that Gag has a higher binding specificity for the HIV-1 Ψ than for the control RNAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of tRNA competition.

claim: The presence of tRNAs partially suppressed the Gag-induced increase in the diffusion constants of the tagged RNAs.
source: We also found that the presence of tRNAs partially suppressed the Gag-induced increase in the diffusion constants of the tagged RNAs (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The presence of tRNAs resulted in a diffusion coefficient similar to that of naked RNAs for MoMLV Ψ and GRPE RNAs.
source: In fact, the diffusion plots for Gag titrations of the MoMLV Ψ and the GRPE RNAs (broken blue and green data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, respectively) show that the presence of tRNAs resulted in a D similar to that of the naked RNAs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The decrease in RNA collapse is not due to interference with binding of Gag to the RNAs.
source: This decrease in RNA collapse is not due to interference with binding of Gag to the RNAs: with the exception of GRPE RNA the quenching plots in the competition experiments exhibited a plateau, just as in the absence of tRNAs (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At Gag concentrations above 100 nM, the degrees of quenching for dimeric HIV-1 Ψ in the presence and absence of tRNAs are indistinguishable from each other.
source: Moreover, at least for the dimeric HIV-1 Ψ at Gag concentrations above 100 nM, the degrees of quenching in the presence and absence of tRNAs are indistinguishable from each other (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: tRNAs may attenuate the Gag-induced increase in D because they are also incorporated into the Gag/RNA complexes.
source: It seems possible that tRNAs attenuate the Gag-induced increase in D because they are also incorporated into the Gag/RNA complexes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: Cooperativity of binding implies that Gag molecules can interact with each other while bound to an RNA.
source: Cooperativity of binding (Figure 2 and Table 1) implies that Gag molecules can interact with each other while bound to an RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the cooperative binding behavior.

claim: The presence of protein-protein interactions could introduce binding hysteresis so that the apparent KD for the competition experiment could depend on the order of addition of the RNAs.
source: It is possible that the presence of protein-protein interactions could introduce binding hysteresis so that the apparent KD for the competition experiment could depend on the order of addition of the RNAs.
evidence: This is speculation based on the cooperative binding behavior.

claim: When tRNAs were added after mixing Gag and monomeric HIV-1 Ψ, the apparent affinity for Ψ was very similar to that in the absence of tRNAs (KDs of 29 vs 26 nM).
source: On the one hand, when the tRNAs were added after mixing Gag and monomeric HIV-1 Ψ (red diamonds), the apparent affinity for Ψ was very similar to that in the absence of tRNAs (red circles) (KDs of 29 vs 26 nM, respectively)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The inverse order of addition of tRNAs showed only a slight decrease in the apparent affinity for monomeric HIV-1 Ψ (KD of 44 nM).
source: while the inverse order of addition showed only a slight decrease in the apparent affinity (KD of 44 nM) (red squares).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The apparent affinity of Gag for GRPE is greatly affected by order of addition of the RNAs.
source: On the other hand, the apparent affinity for the GRPE (green diamonds and squares) is greatly affected by order of addition of the RNAs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The binding hysteresis is greater for the GRPE than for the HIV-1 Ψ.
source: These results show that the binding hysteresis is greater for the GRPE than for the HIV-1 Ψ.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of order of addition.

claim: Addition of tRNAs to pre-incubated Gag/HIV-1 Ψ complexes only affects the size of these complexes at low Gag concentrations.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, addition of tRNAs to pre-incubated Gag/HIV-1 Ψ complexes only affects the size of these complexes at low Gag concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Independent of the order of addition, the presence of tRNAs blocks the Gag-induced collapse of the GRPE RNA.
source: However, independent of the order of addition, the presence of tRNAs blocks the Gag-induced collapse of the GRPE RNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Addition of tRNAs has a weaker effect on Gag/HIV-1 Ψ complexes than on the Gag/GRPE complexes.
source: The difference in the degree of hysteresis in both the binding plots (Figure 4A) and the diffusion plots (Figure 4B) implies that addition of tRNAs has a weaker effect on Gag/HIV-1 Ψ complexes than on the Gag/GRPE complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Gag/HIV-1 Ψ complexes are more stable than Gag/GRPE complexes.
source: This suggests that Gag/HIV-1 Ψ complexes are more stable than Gag/GRPE complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of tRNA addition.

claim: Disruption of the zinc fingers in the NC domain abrogates RNA packaging selectivity.
source: As disruption of the zinc fingers in this domain abrogates RNA packaging selectivity (Aldovini and Young, 1990; Gorelick et al., 1990), these motifs are crucial for gRNA binding and packaging during virion assembly.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The zinc fingers in NC are crucial for gRNA binding and packaging during virion assembly.
source: As disruption of the zinc fingers in this domain abrogates RNA packaging selectivity (Aldovini and Young, 1990; Gorelick et al., 1990), these motifs are crucial for gRNA binding and packaging during virion assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of zinc finger mutations.

claim: In 8N Gag, eight basic residues in the N-terminal region of the MA domain have been replaced with asparagines.
source: In this mutant Gag protein, eight basic residues in the N-terminal region of the MA domain have been replaced with asparagines (Zhou et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a description of the mutant protein, supported by citation.

claim: Removing eight charges in MA reduced the affinity of Gag for monomeric or dimeric Ψ by 2.8 and 2.2-fold, respectively.
source: Table 1 shows that removing these charges in MA reduced the affinity of Gag for monomeric or dimeric Ψ by 2.8 and 2.2-fold, respectively
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Removing eight charges in MA reduced the affinity of Gag for MoMLV Ψ and GRPE RNA by 2.3 and 3.3-fold, respectively.
source: Table 1 shows that removing these charges in MA reduced the affinity of Gag for monomeric or dimeric Ψ by 2.8 and 2.2-fold, respectively, and 2.3 and 3.3-fold for the MoMLV Ψ and GRPE RNA, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The 8N mutation decreased the binding affinity for GRPE RNA, but had little effect on the affinities for the other RNAs.
source: Figure 5A compares the binding plots for wild-type (WT) (solid symbols) and 8N Gag (open symbols). The 8N mutation decreased the binding affinity for GRPE RNA, but had little effect on the affinities for the other RNAs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In cytoplasmic Gag, the MA domain is largely bound to tRNAs.
source: There is evidence that in cytoplasmic Gag, the MA domain is largely bound to tRNAs (Kutluay et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: tRNA had no detectable effect on the apparent binding affinity of 8N Gag for the tagged RNAs.
source: As shown in Figure 5B and Table 1, we found that the tRNA had no detectable effect on the apparent binding affinity of 8N Gag for the tagged RNAs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Table 1.

claim: The eight positive residues in MA that are lacking in 8N Gag are essential for the binding to tRNAs, at least when in competition against viral-derived RNAs.
source: Thus, the eight positive residues in MA that are lacking in 8N Gag are essential for the binding to tRNAs, at least when in competition against these viral-derived RNAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of tRNA on 8N Gag binding.

claim: Binding of 8N Gag to the RNA results in an increase in the diffusion coefficient of the RNA.
source: Figure 5C shows that binding of 8N Gag to the RNA also results in an increase in the diffusion coefficient of the RNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: With the exception of the GRPE RNA, the magnitude of the increase in the diffusion coefficient of the RNAs induced by binding to 8N Gag is greater than that induced by WT Gag.
source: With the exception of the GRPE RNA, the magnitude of the increase in the diffusion coefficient of the RNAs ultimately induced by binding to 8N Gag (open symbols) is greater than that induced by WT Gag (solid symbols).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 8N Gag requires about 1.5–2.8 fold more protein than the wild-type protein to induce collapse in the RNAs.
source: However, 8N Gag requires about 1.5–2.8 fold more protein than the wild-type protein to induce this collapse in the RNAs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: RNA collapse by 8N Gag fits a cooperative model (i.e., nH >1).
source: As with WT Gag, RNA collapse by 8N Gag also fits a cooperative model (i.e., nH >1) (broken lines in Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: While addition of tRNA did not reduce the apparent affinity of 8N Gag for the RNAs, it did increase the size of the resulting complexes.
source: Interestingly, while addition of tRNA did not reduce the apparent affinity of 8N Gag for the RNAs (Figure 5B), it did increase the size of the resulting complexes (see Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5B and 5D.

claim: The eight basic residues that are absent in 8N Gag are necessary for competitive binding by tRNA, but they are not required for incorporation of tRNAs into Gag-RNA complexes.
source: Evidently, the eight basic residues that are absent in 8N Gag are necessary for competitive binding by tRNA, but they are not required for incorporation of tRNAs into Gag-RNA complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of tRNA on binding affinity vs complex size.

claim: The change in D of the RNAs, but not in apparent affinity, of 8N Gag induced by tRNA shows that the increase in D is not an artifact due to Cy5 quenching.
source: It should be noted that the change in D of the RNAs, but not in apparent affinity, of 8N Gag induced by tRNA shows that the increase in D is not an artifact due to Cy5 quenching.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations with 8N Gag.

claim: In solution Gag is in monomer-dimer equilibrium with a KD ≈ 10 μM.
source: In solution Gag is in monomer-dimer equilibrium with a KD ≈ 10 μM (Datta et al., 2007b).

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Gag molecules, including those with the WM mutation, interact with each other when bound to RNA.
source: Thus, Gag molecules, including those with the WM mutation, interact with each other when bound to RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the cooperative binding behavior.

claim: In all titrations, the Gag concentrations were so low (generally ≤300 nM, always ≤600 nM) that Gag dimerization in solution is negligible.
source: It is important to note that in all of our titrations, the Gag concentrations were so low (generally ≤300 nM, always ≤600 nM) that Gag dimerization in solution is negligible (Datta et al., 2007b).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of Gag dimerization affinity and the experimental conditions.

claim: The fact that the WM mutation does not reduce cooperativity suggests that the interactions between RNA-bound Gag molecules do not depend upon the dimer interface.
source: The fact that the WM mutation does not reduce cooperativity suggests that the interactions between RNA-bound Gag molecules do not depend upon the dimer interface.
evidence: This is inferred from the continued cooperativity of WM Gag binding.

claim: While the dimer interface is the only detectable interface for Gag-Gag interaction in solution, other interfaces must also be used in virus assembly.
source: While this is the only detectable interface for Gag-Gag interaction in solution, other interfaces (e.g., in the N-terminal domain of the CA domain (Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2007; von Schwedler et al., 2003; Ganser-Pornillos et al., 2008) and in SP1 (Datta et al., 2011a, Datta et al., 2015) must also be used in virus assembly.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of virus assembly and supported by citations.

claim: Some Gag-Gag interfaces other than the dimer interface could be exposed and contribute to cooperativity when Gag binds RNA.
source: Hence, some of these interfaces could be exposed and contribute to cooperativity when Gag binds RNA in our experiments.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: The binding of WM Gag to the control RNAs was more sensitive to addition of a competitor RNA or increase in salt concentration than that of WT Gag.
source: We also found that the binding of WM Gag to the control RNAs was more sensitive to addition of a competitor RNA or increase in salt concentration than that of WT Gag
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 6 and 9.

claim: The binding of WM Gag to Ψ-containing RNA was relatively resistant to addition of competitor RNA or increase in salt concentration.
source: while the binding of the mutant to Ψ-containing RNA was relatively resistant to these challenges (Figures 6 and 9; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 6 and 9 and Table 1.

claim: The specific Gag/HIV-1 Ψ interactions are strong enough to overcome the destabilization caused by weakening the protein-protein interactions through the dimer interface.
source: These results suggest that the specific Gag/HIV-1 Ψ interactions are strong enough to overcome the destabilization caused by weakening the protein-protein interactions through the dimer interface.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data with WM Gag.

claim: Gag-Gag interaction via the dimer interface significantly strengthens the binding of WT Gag to the control RNAs.
source: In turn, the data imply that Gag-Gag interaction via this interface significantly strengthens the binding of WT Gag to the control RNAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of the WM mutation.

claim: Binding of Gag to RNA exhibits hysteresis.
source: Addition of competitor tRNAs also revealed that binding of Gag to RNA exhibits hysteresis (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Hysteresis is greater with GRPE RNA than with monomeric HIV-1 Ψ RNA.
source: We noted that hysteresis is greater with GRPE RNA than with monomeric HIV-1 Ψ RNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Binding hysteresis is likely associated with the fact that re-equilibration of Gag/RNA complexes, upon addition of a second RNA, requires the dissociation of the initial complex.
source: This binding hysteresis is likely associated with the fact that re-equilibration of Gag/RNA complexes, upon addition of a second RNA, requires the dissociation of the initial complex.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of hysteresis.

claim: Dissociation of Gag/RNA complexes requires disrupting Gag-nucleic acid and Gag-Gag interactions.
source: While binding is driven by Gag-nucleic acid interactions, dissociation of these complexes requires disrupting Gag-nucleic acid and Gag-Gag interactions.
evidence: This is based on general principles of molecular interactions.

claim: Gag re-equilibration, after addition of a second RNA species, must overcome the energetic barrier resulting from breaking Gag-Gag interactions.
source: This implies that Gag re-equilibration, after addition of a second RNA species, must overcome the energetic barrier resulting from breaking Gag-Gag interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding hysteresis observations.

claim: The smaller degree of binding hysteresis for the HIV-1 Ψ RNA, compared to the GRPE RNA, implies that the energetic barrier for re-equilibration is lower in the presence of specific Gag-Ψ interactions.
source: Therefore, the smaller degree of binding hysteresis for the HIV-1 Ψ RNA, compared to the GRPE RNA, implies that the energetic barrier for re-equilibration is lower in the presence of specific Gag-Ψ interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential hysteresis observations.

claim: The ability of a protein to collapse an RNA has previously been reported with capsid proteins of other viruses.
source: The ability of a protein to collapse an RNA (i.e., reduce its hydrodynamic radius and increase its diffusion constant; see Figure 1) has previously been reported with capsid proteins of other viruses (Borodavka et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: RNA collapse presumably occurs when the binding of positively charged regions of the protein to the RNA backbone reduces the electrostatic repulsion within the RNA.
source: Presumably, it occurs when the binding of positively charged regions of the protein to the RNA backbone reduces the electrostatic repulsion within the RNA
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism based on general principles.

claim: RNA collapse by capsid proteins very likely comes into play during assembly of the virus particle.
source: this activity very likely comes into play during assembly of the virus particle.
evidence: This is speculation about the biological significance.

claim: The WM mutation profoundly reduces the ability of HIV-1 Gag protein to collapse RNAs.
source: The fact that the WM mutation profoundly reduces the ability of HIV-1 Gag protein to collapse RNAs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Protein-protein interaction (through the dimer interface) makes an important contribution to RNA collapse.
source: implies that protein-protein interaction (through the dimer interface) makes an important contribution to RNA collapse.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of the WM mutation.

claim: The dependence of RNA collapse on protein-protein interactions is consistent with recently described molecular dynamics simulations on RNA collapse by capsid proteins.
source: The dependence of RNA collapse on protein-protein interactions is also consistent with recently described molecular dynamics simulations on RNA collapse by capsid proteins (Perlmutter and Hagan, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The presence of excess yeast tRNA greatly reduced the magnitude of RNA collapse.
source: It was interesting to note that the presence of excess yeast tRNA greatly reduced the magnitude of RNA collapse (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reduction in RNA collapse by tRNA is true even with 8N Gag, for which RNA binding per se is almost unaffected by tRNA addition.
source: This is even true with 8N Gag (Figure 5), for which RNA binding per se is almost unaffected by tRNA addition (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: tRNA is incorporated into the complexes of Gag and tagged RNA, reducing compaction, via one or more Gag domains other than MA.
source: These observations suggest that tRNA is incorporated into the complexes of Gag and tagged RNA, reducing compaction, via one or more Gag domains other than MA.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations with tRNA and 8N Gag.

claim: The affinity of a Gag molecule for an RNA represents the sum of (I) non-electrostatic interactions; (II) electrostatic interactions; and (III) the interactions between two or more Gag molecules bound to a single RNA molecule.
source: The affinity of a Gag molecule for an RNA represents the sum of (I) non-electrostatic interactions; (II) electrostatic interactions; and (III) the interactions between two or more Gag molecules bound to a single RNA molecule.
evidence: This is a summary of the conclusions based on all the experimental data.

claim: Interactions of the first type (non-electrostatic), mediated largely by the NC zinc fingers, impart specificity for Ψ.
source: Interactions of the first type, mediated largely by the NC zinc fingers, impart specificity for Ψ.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data with SSHC Gag.

claim: To a first approximation, the electrostatic interactions are presumably similar for different RNAs.
source: To a first approximation, the electrostatic interactions are presumably similar for different RNAs
evidence: This is a general assumption about electrostatic interactions.

claim: The basic residues in the MA domain contribute significantly to electrostatic interactions with RNA.
source: our data show that the basic residues in the MA domain contribute significantly to these interactions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with 8N Gag.

claim: It seems likely that the basic character of the NC domain also plays a role in electrostatic interactions with RNA.
source: It seems likely that the basic character of the NC domain also plays a role in these interactions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the basic nature of NC.

claim: The specificity for Ψ is revealed in the presence of mutations that reduce the strength of either electrostatic or Gag-Gag interactions, or by addition of RNAs that compete for these interactions, or in an ionic environment that screens electrostatic interactions.
source: The specificity for Ψ is revealed in the presence of mutations that reduce the strength of either the second or third types of interaction, or by addition of RNAs that compete for these interactions, or in an ionic environment that screens the second type of interaction.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Comparison of the effects of added tRNAs or increased ionic strength upon the apparent affinities of WT and 8N Gag for the labeled RNAs shows that binding to Ψ and non-Ψ RNAs involves both MA and NC domains.
source: Comparison of the effects of added tRNAs or increased ionic strength upon the apparent affinities of WT and 8N Gag for the labeled RNAs (Figures 2B and 3 vs. 5B, and Figures 8 vs. 9) shows that binding to Ψ and non-Ψ RNAs involves both MA and NC domains.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of experimental data.

claim: The current result does not appear to be consistent with a previous binding model in which binding of Gag to Ψ was suggested to involve only NC, while binding to a non-Ψ RNA is driven by interactions with both MA and NC.
source: This result does not appear to be consistent with a previous binding model in which binding of Gag to Ψ was suggested to involve only NC, while binding to a non-Ψ RNA is driven by interactions with both MA and NC (Webb et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work supported by citation.

claim: Webb and co-workers measured Gag/RNA equilibria by doing salt titrations of pre-mixed Gag/RNA complexes (at a fixed Gag:RNA ratio), while the current study titrated a fixed amount of RNA with varying concentrations of Gag at different salt concentrations.
source: Webb and co-workers measured Gag/RNA equilibria by doing salt titrations of pre-mixed Gag/RNA complexes (at a fixed Gag:RNA ratio), while we titrated a fixed amount of RNA with varying concentrations of Gag at different salt concentrations.
evidence: This is a description of methodological differences.

claim: The differences between the experimental approaches are presumably responsible for the resulting discrepancy in binding models.
source: Presumably, the differences between the experimental approaches are responsible for the resulting discrepancy in binding models.
evidence: This is speculation about the reason for the discrepancy.

claim: The apparent affinity of 8N Gag for the dimeric HIV-1 Ψ between 500 and 550 mM NaCl is greater than that of WT Gag.
source: It is somewhat surprising that the apparent affinity of 8N Gag for the dimeric HIV-1 Ψ between 500 and 550 mM NaCl is greater than that of WT Gag (Figure 9—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 3.

claim: The interaction of the WT MA domain with RNAs is presumably almost exclusively electrostatic and is thus negligible at high salt concentrations.
source: However, the interaction of the WT MA domain with RNAs is presumably almost exclusively electrostatic and is thus negligible at these high salt concentrations
evidence: This is speculation based on the nature of MA-RNA interactions.

claim: At high salt concentrations, repulsion between positively charged WT MA domains of two or more RNA-bound Gag molecules raises the energetic cost of RNA-binding, and this repulsion is reduced by the 8N mutations.
source: we surmise that under these conditions, repulsion between positively charged WT MA domains of two or more RNA-bound Gag molecules raises the energetic cost of RNA-binding, and that this repulsion is reduced by the 8N mutations.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the unexpected observation.

claim: Previous studies on protein-nucleic acid binding show that the sensitivity of the binding to an increase in ionic strength is a direct reflection of the net number of charges participating in the binding (Zeff).
source: Previous studies on protein-nucleic acid binding show that the sensitivity of the binding to an increase in ionic strength is a direct reflection of the net number of charges participating in the binding (Zeff) (Webb et al., 2013; Record et al., 1978, 1976; Rouzina and Bloomfield, 1997; Rye-McCurdy et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In previous protein-nucleic acid binding studies, plots of the logarithm of the KD vs. logarithm of the monovalent ion concentration give a straight line, whose slope represents the Zeff.
source: in these experiments, plots of the logarithm of the KD vs. logarithm of the monovalent ion concentration give a straight line, whose slope represents the Zeff.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous biophysical studies.

claim: The bent shape of the log KD vs. log [salt] plots would imply that the Zeff is different under the different ionic regimes.
source: According to the above mentioned studies on protein-nucleic acid interactions, the bent shape would imply that the Zeff is different under the different ionic regimes.
evidence: This is inferred from the bent plots and previous biophysical principles.

claim: It seems likely that the change in slope reflects a conformational change in the Gag protein, which is known to assume very different conformations under different conditions.
source: It seems likely that the change in slope reflects a conformational change in the Gag protein, which is known to assume very different conformations under different conditions (Datta et al., 2007a, 2011b).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations about Gag conformations.

claim: The salt concentration at which the hypothetical conformational change occurs is evidently determined in part by the identity of the RNA.
source: Remarkably, the salt concentration at which this hypothetical change occurs is evidently determined in part by the identity of the RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the different salt concentrations at which the slope changes for different RNAs.

claim: The curves for salt titrations are really straight, and measurements in the lower salt concentrations might be inaccurate at the very high affinities seen with WT Gag and Ψ RNA.
source: It might be proposed that the curves are really straight, and that our measurements in the lower salt concentrations are inaccurate at the very high affinities seen with WT Gag and Ψ RNA.
evidence: This is consideration of an alternative explanation.

claim: The RNA concentration in the experiments (15 nM) is near the measured KDs, and thus the actual KD might be even lower than the results indicate.
source: In fact, the RNA concentration in these experiments (15 nM) is near the measured KDs, and thus we cannot completely exclude the possibility that the actual KD is even lower than our results indicate.
evidence: This is acknowledgment of a potential limitation of the measurements.

claim: The curve for WT Gag and GRPE RNA is also bent, although the binding at each salt concentration is somewhat weaker than with Ψ RNA.
source: However, it is important to note that the curve for WT Gag and GRPE RNA is also bent (Figure 8), although the binding at each salt concentration is somewhat weaker than with Ψ RNA and we have no reason to doubt the accuracy of these measurements.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The fact that a KD could not be measured after the last plotted point for 8N Gag/dimeric Ψ, 8N Gag/GRPE and 310 Gag/dimeric Ψ indicates that there is an abrupt change in the KD at increased salt concentrations.
source: Furthermore, the fact that we were not able to measure a KD after the last plotted point for 8N Gag/dimeric Ψ, 8N Gag/GRPE and 310 Gag/dimeric Ψ indicates that there is an abrupt change in the KD at increased salt concentrations.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability to detect binding at higher salt.

claim: An abrupt change in KD is only possible if the curves for those protein and RNA combinations are bent.
source: Such an abrupt change is only possible if the curves for those protein and RNA combinations are bent.
evidence: This is logical inference from the data.

claim: One might naively expect that as the salt concentration is increased the electrostatic component decreases, ultimately reaching a point at which only the non-electrostatic component remains significant.
source: One might naively expect that as the salt concentration is increased the electrostatic component decreases, ultimately reaching a point at which only the non-electrostatic component remains significant.
evidence: This is a statement of a naive expectation based on general principles.

claim: The naive expectation would produce a curve with a steep slope (i.e., high salt sensitivity) at low salt and a shallow one at high salt; however, the plots show the reverse pattern.
source: This scenario would produce a curve with a steep slope (i.e., high salt sensitivity) at low salt and a shallow one at high salt; however, our plots (Figures 8 and 9) show the reverse pattern.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: The zinc fingers are primarily responsible for non-electrostatic binding.
source: As we have mentioned before, the zinc fingers are primarily responsible for non-electrostatic binding (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The change in slope in the salt titration plots might reflect a change in the conformation of the NC domain, which in turn alters the non-electrostatic interactions of this domain.
source: Perhaps the change in slope reflects a change in the conformation of the NC domain, which in turn alters the non-electrostatic interactions of this domain.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The 'upward bent' curve for salt titration of WT Gag/dimeric Ψ can be generated by using a model in which the KD is a weighted sum of the electrostatic interactions and strong non-electrostatic interactions.
source: Figure 10 shows that the 'upward bent' curve for salt titration of WT Gag/dimeric Ψ (red line and circles) can be generated by using a model (blue line) in which the KD is a weighted sum of the electrostatic interactions (black line and circles) and strong non-electrostatic interactions (solid green line).
evidence: This is a model presented to explain the experimental data, shown in Figure 10.

claim: In the first binding mode (I) the conformation of Gag is such that binding is mostly non-electrostatic.
source: In the first binding mode (I) the conformation of Gag is such that binding is mostly non-electrostatic.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: In the second binding mode (II), the salt-induced conformational change in Gag gradually decreases the contribution of the non-electrostatic interactions.
source: In the second binding mode (II), the salt-induced conformational change in Gag gradually decreases the contribution of the non-electrostatic interactions (dotted green line).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: With 8N Gag/dimeric Ψ, 8N Gag/GRPE, and 310 Gag/dimeric Ψ, only a single slope is visible because binding could not be detected at higher ionic strengths.
source: Again, with 8N Gag/dimeric Ψ, 8N Gag/GRPE, and 310 Gag/dimeric Ψ, only a single slope is visible: this is because we could not detect binding at higher ionic strengths (0.6, 0.45 and 0.5 M NaCl, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The KDs at higher salt concentrations for 8N Gag/dimeric Ψ, 8N Gag/GRPE, and 310 Gag/dimeric Ψ must be >1 µM.
source: The KDs at higher salt concentrations in these cases must be >1 µM.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability to detect binding.

claim: The salt titration curves for 8N Gag/dimeric Ψ, 8N Gag/GRPE, and 310 Gag/dimeric Ψ do have a second slope, but this slope is so steep that measurements could not be made at these high salt concentrations.
source: In other words, these curves do have a second slope, but this slope is so steep that we could not make measurements at these high salt concentrations.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability to detect binding at higher salt.

claim: The distinctive salt resistance of the binding of Gag to Ψ was previously reported by Webb et al.
source: As noted above, the distinctive salt resistance of the binding of Gag to Ψ was previously reported by Webb et al. (Webb et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Webb et al.'s experimental approach was somewhat different from the current study; they could not have detected the bend in the salt titration curves, as the model to which they fitted their salt-titration data assumed a single slope.
source: Their experimental approach was somewhat different from ours; they could not have detected the bend in these curves, as the model to which they fitted their salt-titration data assumed a single slope.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work.

claim: Bent curves in salt titrations were also observed by Record et al., although their experimental system was different.
source: Interestingly, bent curves were also observed by Record et al. (Record et al., 1977), although their experimental system was different from ours in several ways.
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: In general, the data shows that binding of monomeric Ψ and MoMLV Ψ to Gag and its mutants is intermediate between the dimeric HIV-1 Ψ and the GRPE RNA.
source: In general, our data shows that binding of these two RNAs to Gag and its mutants is intermediate between the dimeric HIV-1 Ψ and the GRPE RNA.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Under most experimental conditions the binding affinity of WT, as well as of most mutant Gag proteins, for the dimeric and monomeric HIV-1 Ψ were very similar to each other.
source: Under most experimental conditions the binding affinity of WT, as well as of most mutant Gag proteins, for the dimeric and monomeric HIV-1 Ψ were very similar to each other.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The dimeric RNA always exhibited a higher binding affinity than its monomeric counterpart.
source: Nonetheless, the dimeric RNA always exhibited a higher binding affinity than its monomeric counterpart.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The binding affinity for the dimeric HIV-1 Ψ was considerably higher than that for the monomeric Ψ in the tRNA competition experiments with WM Gag.
source: (Interestingly, the binding affinity for the dimeric HIV-1 Ψ was considerably higher than that for the monomeric Ψ in the tRNA competition experiments with WM Gag.)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The precise start site of genomic RNA affects its ability to dimerize.
source: It was recently reported (Kharytonchyk et al., 2016) that the precise start site of genomic RNA affects its ability to dimerize
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The specific interaction of HIV-1 Gag with HIV-1 Ψ is enhanced by dimerization of the RNA, and would thus, in a genomic RNA molecule, be influenced by the base at which synthesis of a given RNA molecule was initiated.
source: our data suggest that the specific interaction of HIV-1 Gag with HIV-1 Ψ is enhanced by dimerization of the RNA, and would thus, in a genomic RNA molecule, be influenced by the base at which synthesis of a given RNA molecule was initiated.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on dimeric vs monomeric Ψ.

claim: While Gag has similar affinities for different RNAs at near-physiological ionic strength, there are striking differences in the character of the binding: interaction with Ψ-containing RNA has a much larger specific, non-electrostatic component than that with the control RNAs.
source: Taken together, the data show that while Gag has similar affinities for different RNAs at near-physiological ionic strength, there are striking differences in the character of the binding: interaction with Ψ-containing RNA has a much larger specific, non-electrostatic component than that with the control RNAs.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The cellular environment could affect Gag-RNA and Gag-Gag interactions in profound ways, thus allowing for highly specific interactions with the gRNA.
source: In addition, the cellular environment could certainly affect Gag-RNA and Gag-Gag interactions in profound ways (Becker and Sherer, 2017; Lingappa et al., 2014), thus allowing for highly specific interactions with the gRNA.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations.

claim: Ψ-specific interactions could lower the energetic barrier required to nucleate particle assembly more efficiently than binding to other RNAs.
source: We have, however, suggested that Ψ-specific interactions could lower the energetic barrier required to nucleate particle assembly more efficiently than binding to other RNAs (Comas-Garcia et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citation.

claim: The proposed mechanism would explain selective packaging and is consistent with the fact that in the absence of the gRNA, Gag assembles into particles and packages cellular RNAs.
source: This would explain selective packaging and is also consistent with the fact that in the absence of the gRNA, Gag assembles into particles and packages cellular RNAs.
evidence: This is reasoning about the proposed mechanism.

claim: The proposed mechanism is consonant with data implying that the dimeric HIV-1 Ψ supports virion assembly more efficiently than cellular RNAs in vivo.
source: It is also consonant with data implying that the dimeric HIV-1 Ψ supports virion assembly more efficiently than cellular RNAs in vivo (Nikolaitchik et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Results consistent with the proposed hypothesis were recently reported by Carlson et al. and by Dilley et al.
source: Results consistent with this hypothesis were also recently reported by Carlson et al. (Carlson et al., 2016) and by Dilley et al. (Dilley et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.
